notes:
These are verse-by-verse notes on Luke 14. My research tools ran out partway through, so some verses have only one source. I list what I couldn't find at the end.

---

**v. 1**
- Pastor David Guzik (Enduring Word) says Jesus spent time with Pharisees despite their disputes. He did this not to be one of them, but to love them and show them a godly example. He adds that the word for "watching" carried a sense of hostile spying. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-14/

**v. 2**
- Guzik: since the meal was in a leading Pharisee's home, this man was an invited guest. Some believe that he was invited simply to provoke Jesus. He quotes Adam Clarke suspecting a planned trap. Dropsy was a swelling from fluid in the body's tissues. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-14/

**v. 3**
- Guzik: the question was about healing *on the Sabbath*. Jesus was reminding them that there was no command against healing on the Sabbath. What He broke was human tradition built around God's commands, not the commands themselves. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-14/

**v. 4**
- Guzik notes that Jesus' healing involved no ceremony. Because dropsy changed a person's appearance, the man's look would have changed at once, a striking miracle. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-14/

**vv. 5–6**
- Guzik: If it was allowed to help animals on the Sabbath, how much more was it right to heal people who are made in God's image? He quotes G. Campbell Morgan: Jesus appealed to the best in His critics, aiming to save them rather than shame them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-14/

**vv. 7–9**
- Guzik: seating at a meal showed a clear order of honour, and a wedding was the most important social event in Jewish life. Jesus was pointing out the shame that comes when you exalt yourself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-14/

**vv. 10–11**
- Guzik: this is not just good manners. It is the humility of Philippians 2:3, and it is finally fulfilled in eternity. He warns against a subtle pride that takes the low seat in order to be seen as humble. He points to Jesus as the perfect example: He deserved the highest place, took the lowest, and was raised up (Philippians 2:5–11). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-14/

**vv. 12–14**
- Guzik, following Geldenhuys, takes "do not invite" to mean "do not *habitually* invite." It isn't wrong to ever invite your friends, your brothers, and so on; but it is wrong to only invite such people. Full repayment comes at the resurrection, so Jesus is teaching us to live with eternity in view. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-14/

**v. 15**
- Guzik: the guest may have been trying to ease the tension. He was referring to the Messiah's great banquet, spoken of in the Old Testament and called in the New Testament the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-14/

**vv. 16–17**
- Guzik: the date of a banquet was announced well ahead, but the exact time only on the day itself. So these guests had already accepted. He quotes Barclay: to accept beforehand and then refuse on the day was "a grave insult." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-14/
- Matthew Henry reads "all things are now ready" as the time after the Spirit was poured out and the gospel church was planted. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/14-23.html

**vv. 18–20**
- Guzik: the excuses are different but really the same. Their excuses were only a thin veil hiding the fact that they did not want to come. He quotes Morgan: "Back of an excuse is a lack of desire." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-14/

**vv. 21–22**
- Augustine noted that the first group was simply "brought in," not "compelled." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1102173.htm (see v. 23).

**v. 23 — the main verse where readings differ**
- **Traditional reading: earnest persuasion.**
  - Barnes: "compel" means urge them, press them earnestly, one and all. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/14-23.htm
  - Ellicott calls it painful that anyone found in these words approval for using force. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/14-23.htm
  - Bengel: anyone who is simply dragged in by force cannot really be said to "come in." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/14-23.htm
  - Several commentators take the highways and hedges to mean the Gentiles. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/14-23.htm
- **Reformed (Calvin):**
  - Calvin keeps the force of the word. The master orders them to use, as it were, of violence for compelling the attendance of the poor. He applies this to how the gospel itself works: God not only invites but presses us with exhortations, and even threatenings. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/14-23.html and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/luke-14.html
  - A Monergism article says Augustine should not be followed here. Civil penalties cannot produce faith, repentance, or genuine church unity. https://www.monergism.com/donatism
- **Baptist:**
  - Gill: they are compelled not by outward force, but by forcible words, by powerful arguments. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/14-23.html
  - Spurgeon preached a whole sermon on this verse. His tools were words and tears. He also said that he could not compel anyone, but the Spirit of God, who holds the key to the heart, can. https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/sermons/compel-them-to-come-in/
- **Methodist:**
  - Adam Clarke reads it as "prevail on them by the most earnest entreaties." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/14-23.html
  - In the same chapter's notes he says a church that practises persecution is not the Church of Christ. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/luke-14.html
- **Matthew Henry:** compel not by force of arms, but by force of arguments. He calls it absurd to use this verse to force people's consciences. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_014.cfm
- **Catholic (Augustine):**
  - Augustine, writing against the Donatists, used this verse in a different way. "Bring in" stood for the early Church, which was still weak. "Compel" stood for the Church once it had the strength to compel. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1102173.htm
  - He said the Church was following its Lord's example in compelling the Donatists, as Christ had compelled Paul. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1102185.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary also records Anselm's view that God "compels" people by driving them through calamities to take refuge in Him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/14-23.htm

**v. 24**
- Calvin: Christ would rather gather the world's outcasts than ever let such ungrateful people sit at His table. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/14-23.html

**v. 25**
- Guzik: these crowds were attracted to Jesus but perhaps not fully committed. https://enduringword.com/blog-archive/qa-transcripts/a-thought-for-those-deconstructing-christianity-live-qa-with-david-guzik-march-2-2023/

**v. 26**
- **Most common reading: "hate" means love less by comparison.**
  - Clarke (labelled Wesleyan/Methodist on StudyLight) points to Matthew 10:37, "loves… more than me." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/14-26.html
  - GotQuestions points to the "loved" and "hated" wives of Deuteronomy 21:15. https://www.gotquestions.org/hate-father-mother.html
  - Bible.org: to "hate" in our text means "to love less than." It adds that this also means giving up dependence on family. https://bible.org/seriespage/49-how-hate-your-wife-luke-1425-35
- **Other views among older commentators:**
  - The Cambridge Bible says it is less a matter of "love less." When family becomes an actual obstacle to coming to Christ, natural affection must be set aside. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/14-26.htm
  - Bengel goes further and allows a holy hatred in an absolute sense, though without bitterness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/14-26.htm
- **Baptist (Desiring God):** we may be called to do things that look like hatred while longing for our fathers to share eternal life. Jesus speaks in extreme terms to test us. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/if-you-dont-hate-your-father-you-cannot-be-my-disciple
- **Catholic:**
  - Catholic Answers quotes David Lyle Jeffrey calling this Jewish exaggeration for effect. It warns against two traps: loving this life more than God, and despising God's good creation. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/when-jesus-commands-us-to-hate
  - A Catholic homily pushes back against reducing the verse to "priorities." It reads it as pointing to a radically new human family in the risen Christ. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/love-jesus-more-than-justice

**v. 27**
- Guzik: Jesus told the whole crowd what He had told His disciples in Luke 9:23, and this probably horrified His listeners. https://enduringword.com/what-is-required-to-be-saved-live-qa-for-september-19-2024-2/
- GotQuestions: the emphasis is on denying yourself and full surrender. https://www.gotquestions.org/hate-father-mother.html

**vv. 28–32**
- GotQuestions: the builder story explains the hard saying about hating family. The point is to count the cost of being a disciple. https://www.gotquestions.org/hate-father-mother.html
- Guzik: following Jesus costs something, but rejecting Him costs more. https://enduringword.com/what-is-required-to-be-saved-live-qa-for-september-19-2024-2/

**v. 33**
- Guzik: the Greek word for "give up" carried the idea of saying goodbye. We say goodbye to everything we have and entrust it to Jesus. https://enduringword.com/what-is-required-to-be-saved-live-qa-for-september-19-2024-2/

**vv. 34–35**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - The Pulpit Commentary: salt here stands for the spirit of self-sacrifice, self-renunciation. https://biblehub.com/luke/14-34.htm
  - The Expositor's Greek Testament: real disciples are valuable to a corrupt world, while fake disciples are as worthless as salt that has lost its taste. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/14-34.htm
  - Ancient salt was impure, so it really could lose its taste. https://biblehub.com/q/luke_14_34-35__can_salt_lose_flavor.htm
- **Can a real believer lose their "saltiness"? Commentators differ:**
  - George Bliss (An American Commentary, Judson Press) argued that real salt cannot lose its taste. He concluded that no one truly born again ever becomes completely without new life.
  - Coffman replies that ancient salt could and often did lose its taste. So Christ treated losing one's "saltiness" as a real possibility. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/14-34.html
  - Matthew Henry links the verse to Hebrews 6:4–6: it is extremely hard, almost impossible, to win back someone who has fallen away. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_014.cfm
  - Barnes applies it to someone who professes faith but has no grace in their heart. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/14-34.htm
  - One sermon collected on BibleHub states the possibility of a fall from grace outright. https://biblehub.com/sermons/luke/14-34.htm
- **Calvary Chapel connection:** Guzik reads vv. 34–35 as a warning against being a half-hearted follower. He notes that Jesus' strong words drew sinners closer (Luke 15:1). https://enduringword.com/what-is-required-to-be-saved-live-qa-for-september-19-2024-2/

---

**What I couldn't find:**
- **Missing denominational voices:** I found no Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org), Pentecostal-specific, or Orthodox (oca.org) material on this chapter. Guzik is Calvary Chapel rather than Pentecostal.
- **Missing scholarship and popular teaching:** I found nothing from netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, or prosperity or word-of-faith teaching.
- **Thin verses:** I found little on vv. 28–32 beyond what is above, and Precept Austin was not reached.
- **Unread pages:** The Enduring Word page was cut off after v. 20. So for vv. 21–35, Guzik's points come from search excerpts and his other pages. The full Calvin and Clarke chapter pages wouldn't load; their notes on v. 23 come from search excerpts.
